passages.t: The earthly tent and the heavenly house
passages.happening:
Paul has just said that his outer self is wasting away. Now he says what lies beyond it. “Now we know that if the earthly tent we live in is dismantled, we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands” (verse 1).

For now, he groans. “For in this tent we groan, longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling” (verse 2). He does not want to be left without a body. “So while we are in this tent, we groan under our burdens, because we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed, so that our mortality may be swallowed up by life” (verse 4).

God has made them for this, and given a promise of it: “the Spirit as a pledge of what is to come” (verse 5).

So Paul is confident. While he is at home in the body, he is away from the Lord. “For we walk by faith, not by sight” (verse 7). “We are confident, then, and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord” (verse 8).

Either way, his aim is the same: to please the Lord (verse 9). “For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive his due for the things done in the body, whether good or bad” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Paul made tents for a living (Acts 18:3). A tent is a home you can take down. It is good for now, but it is not meant to last. Paul uses it as a picture of the body we live in now: real, our own, but worn and temporary. ‘A building from God’ is the opposite: lasting, made by God, not by human hands.

Then Paul changes the picture to clothes. He longs to ‘put on’ the heavenly dwelling over the present one. He does not want to be ‘unclothed’ or ‘naked’. Many Greeks thought that death set the soul free from the body, and that this was good. Some in Corinth had even said there is no resurrection of the dead (1 Corinthians 15:12). Paul's hope is not to be free of a body. It is to receive a better one. ‘Swallowed up by life’ echoes what he wrote in his first letter: “Death has been swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54).

What happens, then, when a believer dies before Christ returns? Paul's answer here is short. To be ‘away from the body’ is to be ‘at home with the Lord’. He says the same in another letter: “I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed” (Philippians 1:23).

Christians have read these verses in more than one way. Most of the church has held that believers who die are with Christ at once, conscious and at rest, while they wait for the resurrection of the body when Christ returns. On this reading, being ‘unclothed’ is the soul without its body for a time. Paul does not long for that in itself. But being with the Lord makes even that ‘far better’. Some readers think the heavenly house is the resurrection body, given at death. And some Christians hold that the dead are not conscious until the resurrection, a view often called ‘soul sleep’. They point out that the Bible often calls death ‘sleep’, as Paul does (1 Thessalonians 4:13-14), and that the final hope is the resurrection, not the time between. These notes do not choose. All agree that the dead in Christ are safe in God's keeping, and that the end of the story is the raising of the body.

‘The judgment seat’ is the Greek bēma, the raised platform where a judge or governor sat. The Corinthians had seen Paul himself brought before the governor's judgment seat in their city (Acts 18:12).
passages.ot:
The Old Testament also pictures life as a tent. King Hezekiah, near death, said, “My dwelling has been picked up and removed from me like a shepherd’s tent” (Isaiah 38:12). The psalmist calls himself “a foreigner dwelling with You, a stranger like all my fathers” (Psalm 39:12).

Its hope reaches past death. Job says, “Even after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God” (Job 19:26). A psalm says, “As for me, I will behold Your face in righteousness; when I awake, I will be satisfied in Your presence” (Psalm 17:15). Daniel speaks of a day when “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake” (Daniel 12:2).

‘Swallowed up’ comes from Isaiah: “He will swallow up death forever” (Isaiah 25:8).

And the judgment of each person's deeds is an Old Testament teaching too. “For God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil” (Ecclesiastes 12:14).
passages.hard:
What happens to a believer who dies?

Paul gives the heart of it in one line: “away from the body and at home with the Lord” (verse 8). The person is with Christ. That is the comfort these verses hold out, and every Christian tradition holds on to it in some way. But Paul gives few details, and Christians read them differently, as the part above sets out. Most hold that the dead in Christ are with him, aware and at rest, until the resurrection. Some hold that they sleep, unaware, until they are raised. These notes do not choose. The site's doctrine study, ‘Death and the Intermediate State’, sets out each view more fully, and Paul's longer teaching on the resurrection is in 1 Corinthians 15. The Bible Explorer's stop ‘The New Creation’ tells the end of the story simply. On every view, death does not have the last word. The body will be raised.

If you are grieving someone who has died, these verses do not ask you to stop grieving. Jesus wept at his friend's grave (John 11:35). Paul says believers grieve, but not “like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

And what of ‘the judgment seat of Christ’? Paul says believers too will give an account of how they have lived. Readers agree that this is not a second trial of whether a believer is saved: “there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). It is an honest weighing of what each has done. The site's notes on Romans 2:6-11 and 1 Corinthians 3:10-15 set out how Christians understand judgment by works.
passages.asks: Paul says we walk by faith, not by sight. Ask what you are hoping for when you think of death, your own or someone else's. Is it escape from the body, or the Lord himself and a body made new? Then ask how knowing that you will give an account to Christ shapes what you do today, not out of fear, but out of the wish to please him.

passages.t: ‘Christ’s love compels us’, and a new creation
passages.happening:
Because Paul knows what it means to fear the Lord, he tries to persuade people (verse 11). He is not boasting again. He wants to give the church an answer to “those who take pride in appearances rather than in the heart” (verse 12). Whether people think him mad or sane, it is for God and for them (verse 13).

Then Paul gives the reason behind everything he does. “For Christ’s love compels us, because we are convinced that One died for all, therefore all died” (verse 14). “And He died for all, that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for Him who died for them and was raised again” (verse 15).

That changes how Paul sees people. “So from now on we regard no one according to the flesh. Although we once regarded Christ in this way, we do so no longer” (verse 16).

“Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come!” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
‘Those who take pride in appearances’ points again to Paul's rivals, who looked impressive. Paul cares about the heart.

‘Out of our mind’ may answer a charge. Some may have said Paul was unbalanced, too intense, or too taken with visions. Paul says if he seems carried away, it is toward God, and when he speaks plainly, it is for them.

‘Christ's love compels us.’ The word ‘compels’ means to press in on every side, to hold, to drive. Paul is not driven by ambition or fear of his critics. He is driven by what Christ did for him.

‘One died for all, therefore all died.’ Paul means that Christ's death counts for all who belong to him. When he died, they died with him to the old life. So they no longer live for themselves.

‘According to the flesh’ means by merely human standards: status, wealth, looks, background, power. That was how Corinth judged people. Paul once judged Jesus that way too. To him, a crucified man could not be God's Messiah. Then he met the risen Christ, and everything changed. Now he cannot look at anyone the old way.

Verse 17 is short and sharp in Greek. Word for word it says, ‘if anyone in Christ, new creation’. Readers take it in two ways that fit together. The person is made new. And the person now belongs to God's new world, which began when Christ rose from the dead. Both are true for Paul.
passages.ot:
‘New creation’ takes up the promises of the prophets. Through Isaiah God said, “Behold, I am about to do something new; even now it is coming” (Isaiah 43:19). And, “For behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17). Paul's ‘the old has passed away’ echoes Isaiah's “Do not call to mind the former things” (Isaiah 43:18).

The Bible ends where this verse points: “Behold, I make all things new” (Revelation 21:5).

‘Fear the Lord’ is a theme of the whole Old Testament. It does not mean terror. It means a deep reverence that takes God seriously, and it is where wisdom begins.

Paul's words about one who died for all recall Isaiah's servant: “Surely He took on our infirmities and carried our sorrows” (Isaiah 53:4). “He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5).
passages.asks: Paul says he regards no one ‘according to the flesh’. Ask how you size people up: by looks, money, background, usefulness. Ask how it would change if you saw each person as someone Christ died for. And if you belong to Christ, ask what ‘the old’ is that has passed away for you, and what new thing God is doing.

passages.t: Reconciled to God: ambassadors, and the great exchange
passages.happening:
Everything comes from God. “All this is from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation” (verse 18).

Paul says what that means: “that God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, not counting men’s trespasses against them. And He has committed to us the message of reconciliation” (verse 19).

So Paul and his fellow workers speak for God. “Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making His appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ: Be reconciled to God” (verse 20).

Then comes one of the most famous sentences in the Bible. “God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
To reconcile is to make friends again after a quarrel. The word was used in the Greek world for ending enmity between people, families or cities. Paul uses it for God and people. But notice who acts. In the human world, the side that did wrong usually had to make peace. Here God, the one wronged, takes the first step. Paul never says God had to be reconciled to us. He says God reconciled us to himself.

‘Not counting men's trespasses against them.’ To count is a word from keeping accounts. God does not keep a record of debts against those he reconciles.

An ambassador spoke for a king or a city to another people. He carried the ruler's authority and gave the ruler's message, not his own. So Paul says the appeal is God's: ‘as though God were making His appeal through us’. And he says it with feeling: ‘We implore you.’ The Corinthians were already believers, yet their trust in Paul's gospel had been shaken. Paul pleads with them, as with everyone, to be at peace with God.

Verse 21 is built on a balance. Christ, who knew no sin, was made sin. Believers, who were not righteous, become the righteousness of God in him. Christians have called this ‘the great exchange’.
passages.ot:
Behind verse 21 stands the sin offering of the law of Moses. A sinner brought an animal without blemish, laid a hand on its head, and it was killed. “It is a sin offering” (Leviticus 4:24). In Hebrew one word, ḥaṭṭāʾt, means both ‘sin’ and ‘sin offering’. Leviticus 4:3 uses it in both senses in one verse: the priest brings a bull “as a sin offering for the sin he has committed” (Leviticus 4:3). On the Day of Atonement the high priest laid the people's sins on a goat, and “The goat will carry on itself all their iniquities into a solitary place” (Leviticus 16:22).

Isaiah's servant is the clearest picture. “We all like sheep have gone astray, each one has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6). His soul is “made a guilt offering” (Isaiah 53:10).

‘Not counting trespasses’ echoes a psalm: “Blessed is the man whose iniquity the LORD does not count against him” (Psalm 32:2). And God's pleading through his messengers is old too: “I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that the wicked should turn from their ways and live” (Ezekiel 33:11).
passages.hard:
What does ‘God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf’ mean?

First, what all agree on. Jesus ‘knew no sin’: he never sinned. “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth” (1 Peter 2:22). Paul does not mean that Jesus became a sinner. And Christ's death was ‘on our behalf’, for others. As the Nicene Creed confesses, the Son came down ‘for us men and for our salvation’.

But Christians describe the exchange in more than one way. These notes set out the main readings and do not choose.

Some read ‘sin’ here as ‘sin offering’. In Hebrew the same word means both, as the note above shows. Paul says in Romans that God sent his Son “as an offering for sin” (Romans 8:3). On this reading, Christ became the sacrifice that takes sin away.

Others read ‘sin’ in its plain sense: God treated Christ as though he were sin itself. In the Reformed tradition and many Protestant churches, this is read as imputation, a word from keeping accounts. Our sin was counted to Christ, and he bore its judgment; his righteousness is counted to those who trust him. Paul says something similar in Galatians: Christ redeemed us “by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

Others, including many in the Eastern Orthodox churches and some Western readers, put the weight on union with Christ. Christ shared our condition all the way to death, so that those joined to him might share his life and actually be made righteous, changed by God. They note that Paul says ‘become’ the righteousness of God ‘in Him’.

Many hold these readings together. The site's note on Romans 3:21-26 sets out the ways Christians describe what the cross achieved, and stands, as this note does, on the creed that all share.
passages.asks: God took the first step to make peace. Ask whether there is someone you are waiting on to make the first move, and what it would mean to go first. And hear the appeal for yourself, not as pressure but as an invitation: God is not counting trespasses against those who come to him. What would it mean for you to be reconciled to God?
